what_its_for: This medication is a combination birth control pill used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two female hormones — a progestin (norgestrel) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop ovulation (the release of an egg), thicken cervical mucus to keep sperm from reaching an egg, and change the lining of the uterus. It may also be prescribed to help regulate periods or treat certain hormonal conditions.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Try to pick a time that is easy to remember, such as with a meal or at bedtime. Swallow the tablet whole with water. Taking it at the same time every day helps it work best and reduces the chance of side effects like nausea. Your pill pack will have 21 active (hormone) pills and 7 reminder (inactive/placebo) pills. Take the pills in order — do not skip or rearrange them. You will usually get your period during the week you take the reminder pills.
dosing: Take one tablet every day for 28 days, then start a new pack the very next day — even if you are still having your period. Do not skip days between packs. For the first month, use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days, since the pill may not be fully effective right away.
missed_dose: If you miss 1 pill: Take it as soon as you remember, even if that means taking 2 pills in one day. Then continue your regular schedule. No backup birth control is needed. If you miss 2 pills in a row in Week 1 or Week 2: Take 2 pills on the day you remember and 2 pills the next day, then continue one pill per day. Use backup birth control (like condoms) for the next 7 days. If you miss 2 pills in a row in Week 3, or if you miss 3 or more pills at any time: Throw out the rest of the pack and start a new pack that same day. Use backup birth control for 7 days. You may not have a period that month. If you miss a period after missing pills, take a pregnancy test. When in doubt, use backup birth control and call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medication out of reach of children and pets. Do not use pills past the expiration date printed on the pack.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking, especially if you are over 35 years old. Smoking while taking this pill greatly increases your risk of serious heart problems such as blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. Avoid taking this pill with certain medications that can make it less effective, including some seizure medications (like carbamazepine or phenytoin), certain antibiotics (like rifampin), and some herbal products (like St. John's Wort). Always tell every doctor, dentist, and pharmacist that you take birth control pills. Avoid prolonged sitting or bed rest (like long flights) without moving, as this pill can slightly increase the risk of blood clots. Do not take grapefruit juice in large amounts without checking with your pharmacist, as it may affect hormone levels.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you have any of these warning signs — sometimes remembered as ACHES: Abdominal pain (severe); Chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood; Headaches that are severe or different from usual; Eye problems such as blurred vision, flashing lights, or vision loss; Severe leg pain or swelling in one leg. Also contact your doctor if you have: two missed periods in a row (you may need a pregnancy test); signs of a serious allergic reaction (rash, swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing); yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); depression or mood changes; unusual vaginal bleeding; or breast lumps. Tell your doctor before starting this pill if you have a history of blood clots, stroke, heart disease, high blood pressure, migraines with aura, liver disease, breast cancer, or if you are breastfeeding.
when_it_works: When taken correctly every day, this pill is about 99% effective at preventing pregnancy. It takes about 7 days to become fully effective after you start taking it. If you start on the first day of your period, it may be effective right away. Pregnancy protection depends on taking the pill consistently — missing pills increases your risk of becoming pregnant.
special_populations: Women over 35 who smoke should NOT use this medication due to a very high risk of serious heart problems. This pill is NOT recommended if you are pregnant, think you may be pregnant, or are breastfeeding a newborn (it can reduce milk supply). Women with a history of blood clots, stroke, heart attack, uncontrolled high blood pressure, certain types of migraines, liver disease, or certain cancers should not use this pill — talk to your doctor about safer alternatives. Teenagers can use this medication, but a doctor should first confirm that periods have already started regularly. Older women approaching menopause should discuss risks and benefits with their doctor. If you have diabetes, kidney disease, or high cholesterol, your doctor will monitor you more closely while you use this medication.
